issue.issue_text: Whether the election of the appellant was wrongly set aside by the Tribunal.

facts: The appellant's election was set aside by a majority decision of an election Tribunal.
The basis for setting aside the election was the Tribunal's finding that the appellant held an 'office of profit under the Government'.
The appellant's appointment was under a Committee, which is a statutory body.
The appellant's salary was paid from the funds of the Durgah Endowment, not from the revenues of the Government.
law: An appointment under a statutory body is not considered an appointment by or under the control of the Government.
If a salary is not paid out of government revenues, the position is not considered an office of profit under the Government.
application: The Supreme Court found that the majority of the Tribunal had erred in its conclusion.
The Court determined that since the appellant was appointed by a statutory committee and his salary was paid by the Durgah Endowment, he did not hold an office of profit under the Government.
The Court agreed with the dissenting opinion of the Tribunal's Chairman, stating that it laid down the correct legal position.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the election of the appellant was wrongly set aside by the Tribunal. Consequently, the Court allowed the appeal and overturned the Tribunal's order.

issue.issue_text: Whether sections 207 and 207A of the Code of Criminal Procedure are discriminatory and contravene Article 14 of the Constitution by prescribing a different, less advantageous procedure for cases initiated on a police report.

facts: The appellants were committed for trial to the Court of Session based on a police report.
The magistrate followed the procedure laid down in section 207A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as required by section 207.

The appellants argued that this procedure was discriminatory and less advantageous compared to the procedure for cases initiated on private complaints (governed by other sections in Chapter XVIII of the Code).
They contended that this difference in procedure violated their right to equality under Article 14 of the Constitution.
law: The legal test for determining if a law violates Article 14 is whether the classification it creates is reasonable.
A reasonable classification must be based on a relevant consideration that distinguishes the groups being classified.
This classification must also have a rational connection to the objective the legislature aims to achieve.
application: The Court acknowledged that the law prescribes two different procedures for commitment proceedings: one for cases based on a police report and another for cases initiated otherwise.

It identified the basis for this classification as the fact that cases initiated on a police report have already undergone a "previous inquiry by a responsible public servant whose duty it is to discover crime".
The Court determined that the objective of the legislation was to ensure a "speedy trial of offences with the least possible delay."

It reasoned that the classification is directly and reasonably related to this objective. Since a police investigation has already occurred, a more streamlined commitment procedure is justified to expedite the process and bring the accused to trial sooner.
The Court also noted that the procedural differences only exist at the commitment stage and do not affect the procedure at the actual trial, which remains the same for both classes of cases.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the classification between cases initiated on a police report and other cases was reasonable and had a clear connection to the legislative object of ensuring a speedy trial. Therefore, sections 207 and 207A were not discriminatory, did not contravene Article 14 of the Constitution, and were constitutionally valid. The Court rejected the appellants' contention.

arguments.issue_text: Whether sections 207 and 207A of the Code of Criminal Procedure are discriminatory and contravene Article 14 of the Constitution by prescribing a different, less advantageous procedure for cases initiated on a police report.
appellant_arguments: Sections 207 and 207A of the Code create two different procedures for commitment proceedings: one for cases initiated on a police report and another for all other cases.
The procedure for cases initiated on a police report (under s. 207A) is less advantageous to the accused compared to the procedure for other cases.

Accused persons in cases under s. 207A are denied facilities available to others. For example, under s. 208(3) an accused can apply to compel witness attendance, but the corresponding s. 207A(2) only mentions the prosecution.
In proceedings on a complaint, the accused has three potential stages at which they can be discharged, which is more advantageous than the procedure under s. 207A.
respondent_arguments: The classification between the two procedures is reasonable and based on a relevant consideration: whether a prior inquiry has been conducted by a responsible public servant (the police).
The legislative object of this classification is to ensure a speedy trial of offences with the least possible delay, which is a valid goal.
While the commitment procedures differ, these differences do not affect the procedure at the actual trial, which remains the same for both classes of cases.
The classification is not unreasonable and has a clear relation to the object of the legislation, which is a more speedy trial.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A legislative classification that prescribes different pre-trial commitment procedures for criminal cases, one for those instituted on a police report and another for those instituted otherwise, does not violate Article 14 of the Constitution. Such a classification is permissible when it is founded on an intelligible differentia—the presence or absence of a prior investigation by a public agency—which has a rational relation to the legislative object of achieving a speedy trial.
obiter: A discretionary power is not necessarily discriminatory.
It is the avowed policy of the Legislature and in the general interest of administration of justice that crimes should be investigated and criminals brought to justice as expeditiously as possible.
The principle of classification of offences and of different categories of cases relating to the trial of offences is a well-established rule of criminal procedure.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Applying the principles laid down by this Court to the case in hand to judge whether or not there has been objectionable discrimination, there could not be the least doubt that the Legislature has provided for a clear classification between the two kinds of proceedings at the commitment stage based upon a very relevant consideration, namely, whether or not there has been a previous inquiry by a responsible public servant whose duty it is to discover crime and to bring criminals to speedy justice. This basis of classification is clearly connected with the underlying principle of administration of justice that an alleged criminal should be placed on his trial as soon after the commission of the crime as circumstances of the case woi;ld permit. This classification cannot be said to be unreasonable and not to have any relation to the object of the legislation, namely, a more speedy trial of offences without any avoidable delay.
legal_tests_applied: In order, however, to pass the test of permissible classification two conditions must be fulfilled, namely, (I) that the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group and (II) that that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question.
why_appellant_lost: The court found that while the commitment procedures differed, these differences did not impact the actual trial procedure, which remained the same for both classes of cases. The text states: 'At the threshold, it is pertinent to observe that these provisions have not in any way affected the procedure at the trial. After a case has been committed to a Court of Session, the procedure for the trial of offences in either class of cases, remains the same.'

The court rejected the premise that a more elaborate procedure is always more advantageous to the accused, suggesting that a speedier process can be in the interest of an innocent person. The court reasoned: 'But is it always to the advantage of an accused person that there should be an elaborate procedure before such a magistrate and not a summary one? ... If a person has been falsely or wrongly accused of an offence, .it is in his interest that he should get himself declared innocent by a competent court as early as possible.'
why_respondent_won: The court determined that the classification between cases initiated by a police report and those initiated otherwise is based on a reasonable and relevant consideration: whether a prior investigation has been conducted by a responsible public servant. The court stated the classification is 'based upon a very relevant consideration, namely, whether or not there has been a previous inquiry by a responsible public servant whose duty it is to discover crime and to bring criminals to speedy justice.'

The court found a clear and rational nexus between the basis of the classification and the legislative objective of ensuring a speedy trial. The court held: 'This classification cannot be said to be unreasonable and not to have any relation to the object of the legislation, namely, a more speedy trial of offences without any avoidable delay.'

The court justified the more elaborate procedure for complaint cases by noting the need for greater judicial vigilance when a case has not been pre-vetted by the police, in order to prevent 'private vendetta'. The court reasoned: 'The magistrate has got, therefore, to be more vigilant in seeing that private vendetta and considerations other than those of vindicating justice, are not allowed to interfere with the administration of public justice. Hence, the procedure laid down in section 208 and the sections following that section, naturally gives greater facilities to persons accused of an offence, to vindicate their character.'
policy_considerations: It is the avowed policy of the Legislature and there can be no doubt that it is in the general interest of administration of justice, that crimes should be investigated and criminals brought to justice as expeditiously as circumstances of the case would permit.

The Legislature, in its wisdom, has proceeded on the basis that it is primarily the function of the State through its police officers who are charged with the duty of preventing the commission of crime and of bringing offenders. to justice, to prosecute ciriminals or alleged criminals in serious cases, that is to say, cases involving not only personal injury to the complainant but also public peace and order.
